entities.summary:
Jean de Liège (c. 1330–1381) stands as a pivotal figure in late Gothic sculpture, primarily active in the French royal court during the tumultuous Hundred Years' War. Hailing from the Prince-Bishopric of Liège, a region renowned for its artistic heritage, he rose to prominence as a master sculptor specializing in funerary monuments and effigies for the French monarchy and high nobility. His workshop's innovative approach to tomb sculpture, characterized by a heightened naturalism and emotional depth, profoundly influenced the artistic currents of northern Europe, bridging the stylistic traditions of the Meuse valley with the burgeoning International Gothic style that would dominate the late 14th and early 15th centuries.

Appointed royal sculptor to King Charles V of France around 1364, Jean de Liège's career flourished under royal patronage. His most significant commissions included the tomb effigies for Charles V and his queen, Jeanne de Bourbon, at the Basilica of Saint-Denis, completed between 1364 and 1374. These works, along with the tomb of Duchess Blanche of France and the effigy of Marie de France, attest to his mastery in rendering individual likenesses and drapery with remarkable realism. Beyond royal projects, he undertook numerous commissions for the French aristocracy, establishing a highly productive atelier in Paris that employed and trained many apprentices and assistants, thus disseminating his distinctive sculptural vocabulary.

entities.summary:
Jean de Liège (c. 1330–1381) stands as a pivotal figure in 14th-century European sculpture, renowned for his refined naturalism and profound emotional expression, primarily active in France under significant royal patronage. Hailing from Liège in the Prince-Bishopric of Liège, a region then part of the Holy Roman Empire but culturally linked to the Low Countries, his career flourished within the artistic orbit of the French Valois court. His work bridged the stylistic conventions of earlier Gothic sculpture with a nascent realism that would characterize the late medieval period, making him a crucial precursor to the International Gothic style.

His most celebrated commissions include the effigies for the tomb of King Charles V and his wife Jeanne de Bourbon at the Abbey of Saint-Denis, executed between 1364 and 1372, which exemplify his mastery of portraiture and drapery. He also created the poignant recumbent figure of Marie de France, daughter of Charles V, for the now-destroyed Abbey of Poissy, and contributed to the elaborate funerary monument of the heart of Charles V in Rouen Cathedral. Beyond royal projects, Jean de Liège received commissions from powerful aristocrats, including the monumental tomb of Philippe d'Artois at the Jacobins in Paris and works for Jean, Duke of Berry, such as the 'Vierge dorée' of the Sainte-Chapelle de Bourges, showcasing his versatility across different scales and materials.
